# Handling a returned library book

When a borrower hands back a book, the library does more than put it on a
shelf. Staff follow a short routine so that the catalogue always matches what
is physically in the building, and so that damaged copies do not quietly return
to circulation. This text describes that routine and then the states a single
copy passes through during its life in the library.

## Checking in a returned copy

Staff carry out the routine in this order.

1. Scan the barcode inside the cover. The catalogue shows which borrower had
   the copy and whether it was overdue.
2. If the copy was overdue, record the number of days late. The system works out
   any fine from that number, and staff do not calculate it by hand.
3. Inspect the copy for damage. Look at the spine, the corners, the pages for
   marks or water stains, and the barcode label itself.
4. Decide what the inspection found. If the copy is undamaged, continue to step
   5. If it is lightly damaged, for example a loose page or a torn label, send
   it to the repair table and skip to step 7. If it is badly damaged or has
   pages missing, set it aside for withdrawal and skip to step 7.
5. Check whether another borrower has reserved the copy. If so, place it on the
   reservation shelf with a slip carrying the waiting borrower's name, and
   notify that borrower. If not, continue to step 6.
6. Place the copy on a sorting trolley. At the end of the shift a colleague
   wheels the trolley to the stacks. If the shelf mark on the spine is missing
   or does not match the catalogue entry, go back to step 1 and scan the copy
   again so the record can be corrected before it is shelved.
7. Update the catalogue status to match where the copy now is, and put the
   borrower's record in order by clearing the loan.

Step 6 is the only place where work returns to an earlier step. The return
loop exists because a wrong shelf mark would send the copy to the wrong
place, and a book on the wrong shelf is as good as lost.

## The life of one copy

A copy is always in exactly one named state, and the catalogue shows which one.
When the library acquires a copy and enters it into the catalogue, its state is
Available. It stays Available while it sits on its shelf and anyone may borrow
it.

When a borrower takes it out, the state becomes On loan. If the due date passes
without a return, the state becomes Overdue, and it returns to On loan only if
the borrower renews it. Returning an Overdue copy ends the loan, as in the
routine above.

If another borrower has asked for a copy that is On loan, the copy moves to
Reserved once it is returned, and it stays there until the waiting borrower
collects it or the collection period lapses. After collection it is On loan
again. If the collection period lapses, the copy goes back to Available.

A copy that fails inspection moves to Under repair, and it returns to Available
when the repair is done. A copy judged beyond repair becomes Withdrawn, which is
the end of its life in the catalogue: a withdrawn copy never becomes Available
again. A copy that cannot be found after a stocktake becomes Missing, and it
may return to Available if it turns up.
